question: A request to `DELETE /invoices/17` carries a valid, unexpired access token, but the user's role isn't allowed to delete invoices. Which status code fits best?
options: `400 Bad Request`
`401 Unauthorized`
`403 Forbidden`
`405 Method Not Allowed`
`409 Conflict`
explanation:
`403` means the server knows who the caller is and refuses anyway; authenticating again won't help. `401`, despite its name, means the request lacks valid credentials, and it should come with a `WWW-Authenticate` header that tells the client how to authenticate. `405` is for a method the resource doesn't support for anyone.

Some APIs deliberately return `404` to hide that a resource exists, but that is a privacy choice, not the standard meaning.

question: Which HTTP methods are idempotent according to the HTTP specification? Select all that apply.
options: `GET`
`POST`
`PUT`
`DELETE`
`PATCH`
explanation:
Idempotent means sending the same request several times has the same effect on the server as sending it once, which is why clients and proxies may safely retry such requests.

`PUT` replaces the resource with the representation sent, and repeating a `DELETE` leaves the resource deleted; the status code can differ (say `404` the second time), which doesn't matter. `POST` usually creates something new each time. `PATCH` isn't idempotent by definition, because a patch can be relative, such as "append this item". `HEAD`, `OPTIONS` and `TRACE` are idempotent too.

question: A response carries `Cache-Control: no-cache` and an `ETag` header. What may the browser do with it?
options: Nothing: it must not store the response anywhere
Reuse it without contacting the server until the tab is closed
Store it in the browser cache, while shared caches such as CDNs must not store it
Store it, but check with the server before every reuse, for example with `If-None-Match`, and use the stored copy if the server answers `304`
explanation:
`no-cache` means "don't reuse without revalidating". The browser may keep the response and send a conditional request each time; a `304 Not Modified` lets it reuse the stored body without downloading it again.

Forbidding storage altogether is `no-store`, which is what sensitive responses need. Letting only the browser, but not shared caches, store a response is `private`.

question:
A single-page app at `https://app.example.com` runs:

```js
const res = await fetch("https://api.example.com/me", { credentials: "include" });
```

The API responds `200` with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` and no other CORS headers. What happens?
options: It works, because `*` allows every origin, with or without credentials
The browser blocks the page from reading the response; for credentialed requests the server must return the exact origin `https://app.example.com` and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`
Nothing is blocked, because both hosts are under `example.com` and therefore count as the same origin
The request succeeds, but the browser strips the cookies from it because of the wildcard
explanation:
Two hosts are different origins even when they share a parent domain. For a request made with `credentials: "include"`, the CORS check fails if `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` is `*` or if `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` is missing, so the `fetch` promise rejects with a `TypeError`.

The cookies are still sent, and the server may well have done the work; the page just can't read the answer, because CORS is enforced by the browser. The fix is to echo an allow-listed origin, send `Vary: Origin`, and allow credentials.

question:
`https://bank.example` sets this cookie:

```http
Set-Cookie: sid=abc123; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
```

Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: Scripts on `bank.example` can't read it through `document.cookie`
It is sent when a user on `https://news.example` clicks an ordinary link to `https://bank.example/account`
It is sent when a page on `https://evil.example` auto-submits a hidden `<form method="POST">` to `https://bank.example/transfer`
It is sent with an `` embedded in a page on `https://evil.example`
The browser won't send it to `http://bank.example`
Because it is `HttpOnly`, an XSS bug on `bank.example` can no longer make authenticated requests as the user
explanation:
`HttpOnly` hides the cookie from JavaScript, and `Secure` restricts it to HTTPS. `SameSite=Lax` sends the cookie on cross-site **top-level navigations with safe methods**, such as following a link, but not on cross-site subresource requests (images, iframes, `fetch`) and not on a cross-site `POST`, which is what stops the classic CSRF form.

`HttpOnly` doesn't make XSS harmless: injected script can still send same-origin requests, and the browser attaches the cookie to them. It only stops the script from reading and stealing the cookie's value.
